related_questions.question: Is HIV a retrovirus that infects and colonizes?
related_questions.snippet: HIV is a retrovirus that infects cells of the human immune system (mainly CD4-positive T-cells and macrophages—key components of the cellular immune system) and destroys or impairs their function. Infection with this virus results in the progressive depletion of the immune system, leading to immunodeficiency.

related_questions.question: Which system of the body does HIV infect?
related_questions.snippet: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is a virus that attacks the immune system. (The immune system fights infections and diseases in a person's body.) Over time, HIV weakens a person's immune system so it has a very hard time fighting diseases.

related_questions.question: What is a retrovirus that infects cells of the immune system?
related_questions.snippet: HIV is a retrovirus that infects humans. The virus attaches itself to specific white blood cells, called CD4 T cells. These cells are important components of the immune system, helping to fight infections in the body.

text_blocks.snippet: HIV, or Human Immunodeficiency Virus, is found in the body fluids of an infected person. These fluids include blood, semen, pre-ejaculate, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, and breast milk. HIV is not found in urine, sweat, or saliva. HIV can be transmitted through unprotected sexual contact, sharing needles, or from mother to child during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding.
snippet_highlighted_words: in the body fluids of an infected person

list.title: Body Fluids:
list.snippet: HIV primarily exists in the blood, semen, pre-ejaculate, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, and breast milk of an infected individual.

list.title: Sexual Transmission:
list.snippet: The virus can be transmitted through unprotected anal, vaginal, or oral sex.

list.title: Needle Sharing:
list.snippet: Sharing needles, syringes, or other equipment used to prepare drugs for injection is a significant risk factor.

list.title: Mother-to-Child Transmission:
list.snippet: HIV can be passed from a mother to her child during pregnancy, childbirth, or through breastfeeding.

list.title: Not Transmitted Through:
list.snippet: HIV is not transmitted through casual contact such as kissing, hugging, or sharing food. It is also not transmitted through mosquitoes or other insects.

list.title: Organ and Tissue Transplantation:
list.snippet: HIV can be transmitted through organ and tissue transplantation, but this is rare due to screening measures.

list.title: Medical Injections:
list.snippet: In some regions, unsafe medical injections contribute to HIV transmission, but this is becoming less common due to improved safety practices.
